description: Does a WCF client call work on Linux? Keyed by target framework, platform, binding (config element name), effective security mode and the credential type that mode uses ('None' when the mode is None; '*' matches any; the most specific entry wins). Verdicts: compatible, requires_change, incompatible; each that is not compatible says what must change and who changes it (we, backend_owner, or we_or_backend_owner). Same sourcing and confirmation flow as wcf-client-support: every entry names its sources, may carry probe results, and must be confirmed by a person before a report built on it goes to a client.

sources.title: WCF Features in .Net Core 2.1 - the dotnet/wcf supported-features chart
sources.note: The newest chart dotnet/wcf publishes, written for .NET Core 2.1. Its Linux column is read for the platform verdict: NetTcpBinding, Http, Https, Tcp, Kerberos/TCP, Kerberos/HTTP and Certificate supported; NTLM not supported.

sources.title: dotnet/wcf release v1.0.0-rc2
sources.note: Windows stream security (NegotiateStream): seamless on Windows; on other OSes, available with Kerberos authentication, dependent on the OS's Kerberos implementation (MIT GSSAPI on Ubuntu and Debian), whose components must be installed.

sources.title: dotnet/wcf release v2.0.0
sources.note: Windows authentication is now supported by Http transport on Linux and OS X (#946).

sources.title: dotnet/wcf release v6.2.0
sources.note: System.ServiceModel.UnixDomainSocket added as an alternative to NetNamedPipe that works on all supported platforms.

sources.title: dotnet/wcf release-notes package list
sources.note: The WCF client ships System.ServiceModel.Primitives, Http, NetTcp, NetNamedPipe, NetFramingBase, Duplex, Security, Federation and UnixDomainSocket. No package provides MSMQ, peer, web (REST) or dual-HTTP bindings.

entries.basis: chart Linux: NTLM not supported

fix.change: the backend's owner must accept a credential a Linux caller can present: Kerberos (Negotiate), a certificate, a username or a token

entries.basis: chart Linux: Kerberos/HTTP supported; release v2.0.0: Windows authentication on Http transport on Linux; release v1.0.0-rc2: Kerberos on Linux needs the OS's GSSAPI components
entries.caveat: Windows credentials negotiate Kerberos on Linux. On our side: a Kerberos client in the image (krb5 and GSSAPI), a krb5.conf for the domain, and credentials or a keytab for the calling identity. Otherwise the backend's owner offers a credential a Linux caller can present without the domain: a certificate, a username or a token. Which applies is decided by a probe in a Kerberos environment.

fix.change: Kerberos configuration on our side, or a credential change by the backend's owner
